First, we get the RS data set and clean it up.

Note, that this default RS data set in the rENA package is a MESS. There are duplicated lines, and there are no mentors included in the data. We should probably do something about that, see [issue here](https://gitlab.com/epistemic-analytics/qe-packages/rENA/-/issues/39)



# Data Conversion

Now, we need to convert the timestamps in the RSdata set into useable numbers.

Note that we also need to get an estimate of the time gap between utterances in order to convert from data about referents to times.

We have data on referents from Michael Tscholl

His data showed:

Furthest referent	| Percent
------------------|-------------
0                 | 1
1                 | 0.975961538
2                 | 0.65625
3                 | 0.355769231
4                 | 0.180288462
5                 | 0.048076923
6                 | 0.019230769
7                 | 0.014423077
8                 | 0.004807692
9                 | 0


These is a survivorship analysis. So 18% of lines had their furthest referent 4 lines OR FEWER back in the data.

We thus use a WEIGHTING of .18 for an utterance that is 4 turns back. Why? Because ON AVERAGE, that is the expected 
value of the contribution from an utternace that far back.

But here we need times, so we find the average time between utterances -- leaving out the gaps between days.

The analysis below (see histogram) showed that there were a lot of outliers in the time lags: the mean was 2.8 minutes, 
which by inspeection of the data seemed like a long time. 

The mean lag for chats less than 10 minutes apart was .78, which seemed like a more reasonable estimate, given the data.

Tschol; suggested a window size of 4 or 5, with the idea that there were few additional chats that were going to be
included after that, and we would likely be including things in the recent temporal context that were not actually
referents.

This would make the average RCT something on the order of 3-4 minutes, which, again, seems reasonable.

```{r convertTimestamps}

#convert timestamps
d$time = convert.time( as.character(d$Timestamp), units = "minutes")

#I used this to get time lags not counting changes in days
#this gave me an "average" time between turns of talk

#put in NAs to cover changes in day
d$timeLag = rep(NA, nrow(d))
for(x in 1:(nrow(d)-1)) {
  if(d$GameDay[x] == d$GameDay[x+1]){
    #this assigns, for each row, the time it is BEHIND or BEFORE the next row
    d$timeLag[x] = d$time[x+1] - d$time[x]
  }
}
rm(x)

hist(d$timeLag)
mean(na.omit( d$timeLag[d$timeLag] ))
hist(d$timeLag[d$timeLag<10])
mean(na.omit( d$timeLag[d$timeLag<10] ))
```

This meant that we needed a decay function that modeled this curve:

Minutes |	Decay
--------|--------
0.00    |  1
0.78    |  0.975961538
1.56    |  0.65625
2.34    |  0.355769231
3.12    |  0.180288462
3.90    |  0.048076923
4.68    |  0.019230769
5.46    |  0.014423077
6.24    |  0.004807692

I cheated a bit for now and put the data in Excel, and used a polynomial trendline, coming up with 

$$
y = -0.0059x^4 + 0.0806x^3 - 0.3186x^2 + 0.1178x + 1
$$

$$
R^2 = 0.9948
$$

We'll have to develop some r function to do this kind of estimation at some point. The current version is wildly overfit, but in this case that isn't really so bad, as we are really just INTERPOLATING rather than EXTRAPOLATING from this function.

Note that I am not using an exponential decay function because it doesn't fit the data as well. The data looks something like this:

```
|
|
•  •  
|     •
|         •
|               •
|______________________•__________•
```

The little plateau makes it hard to fit with an exponential. Not saying we shouldn't do that anyway, but for this experiment it didn't seem like the right choice.


```{r determineDecayFunction}

#from tscholl
#modeled in Excel for now... will need to write a function to generate this equation from raw data

#y = -0.0059x4 + 0.0806x3 - 0.3186x2 + 0.1178x + 1
#R² = 0.9948

#specific function for these decay values
decay.function = function(x) return(-0.0059*x^4 + 0.0806*x^3 - 0.3186*x^2 + 0.1178*x + 1)

```

# Test and Verify Decay 

Next, I developed functions to compute the decay for given a time for a current event (now) and a time or times for events in the past (event.time).

The function get.decay works with just a single decay function. 

As the example shows, get.decay.modes works if you specify a named LIST of funcitons that correspond to some data column with information about the modalities in the data (eg, page view v chat).

Thanks to Cody for the call_eq function that this uses. That was a pain to figure out for me.

```{r}

#TEST code 
my.modes = c("m2", "m3", "m2", "m2")
my.test.decay = list()
my.test.decay$m2 = function(x) return(2*x)
my.test.decay$m3 = function(x) return(3*x)

get.decay.modes(now = 5, event.time = 1:4, modes = my.modes, decay.function = my.test.decay)
get.decay.modes(now = 3, event.time = 1:2, decay.function = decay.function)

rm(my.modes)
rm(my.test.decay)
 
```

# Find Unit Context

OK, so now we need to find the CONTEXTS for each unit of analysis in the data. The context is basically the horizon of observation (HOO) for each unit -- the things (chats, documents, galvanic skin response) that they are aware of and thus can "respond" to. (We are using "aware of" in a general sense here. We are not *directly* aware of our galvanic skin response, but we do respond to the stress it reflects.)

# Test Attenuation

Here we test the function on an attenuated data set (easier to check outputs). You can remove the limit on the size of the data set in the first line below.

For the test, we assign a set of fake "modes" to the data (in this casee, chat and page view). 

The get context function also requires that you supply the data columns for users. This is so that it is possible to get contexts for only some of the users.

We assign HOO rules to a list of lists.

The first level has an (unnamed) list for each rule.

The next level has a NAMED list where each name is the column the condition should apply to, and the content of the list
is a string where options are...
   ...<UNIT>, which is replaced by the value of the individual unit 
               for which context is being constructed
   ...any regex
   
The funciton will include rows of data that match ALL of the conditions of ANY rule.

The test here shows two cases:

1. Subset by condition and group, as in regular ENA
2. Subset by condition and group, but with ALL data modes for the unit and only chats for confederates


```{r getHOOcontexts}

#add fake "communication types" to data for hoo

#Do this only once so that it stays stable
if(!is.object("CommunicationType")){
    CommunicationType = sample(x = c("chat","view"), size = nrow(d), replace = T, prob = c(.8, .2))
    d.plus = cbind(CommunicationType, d)
}

#create reduced data set
d.run = d.plus[1:100, ]

#specify hoo rules as list of lists
#note that options here are...
#   ...<UNIT>, which is replaced by the value of the individual unit 
#               for which context is being constructed
#   ...any regex
my.hoo.usualENA = list()
my.hoo.usualENA[[1]] = list(Condition = "<UNIT>", GroupName = "<UNIT>")

my.hoo.TMA = list()
my.hoo.TMA[[1]] = list(Condition = "<UNIT>", GroupName = "<UNIT>", CommunicationType = "chat")
my.hoo.TMA[[2]] = list(Condition = "<UNIT>", UserName = "<UNIT>")

#set units
#get all possible units in the set
my.units = unique(d.run[,c("Condition", "UserName")])
#use only a few for this analysis
my.units = my.units[1:3,]

#generate contexts for this data: REGULAR ENA
hoos.regular = get.contexts(units = my.units, data = d.run, hoo.rules = my.hoo.usualENA)
#generate contexrs for this data: TMA
hoos.TMA = get.contexts(units = my.units, data = d.run, hoo.rules = my.hoo.TMA)

#show results

#show full output for one 
## clm - commented out for now, makes output unreadable/too long
#hoos.regular
##hoos.TMA

#compare these two (first panels in the output)
#Notice there is no rows for VIEW for brandon or akash in the TMA version
#because they are is not the unit. But there are two for Steven because he is the unit
# clm - using head() to reduce ouput
head(hoos.regular$contexts$`FirstGame::steven z`$context)
head(hoos.TMA$contexts$`FirstGame::steven z`$context)


#use REGULAR ENA going forward so it is easier to check values
these.hoos = hoos.regular

```

# Make a Decay Model

So, now we're ready to make a decay model.

The basic approach of the model is to loop over the contexts from the get.contexts function. Each context is associated 
with one unit of analysis, and carries all of the rows of data that the unit can "see".

So, we do some initializing of variables, and then loop over the contexts. 

We start by pulkling out all of the rows that have no codes in them -- they don't contribute anything to the analysis, 
and we don't need them as "spacer" rows to track windows. 

In each context, we pull out the "receiving" rows -- that is, the rows that belong to the unit -- and loop over those. 
If there aren't any (after pulling out the zero rows) then we skip the unit.

For each response row, we find the rows in the context that happen before the response. These are the ground. (We can 
also specify a maximum time back in time if the data file is very large and we want to save a little processing time.)

We then apply the decay function to the ground codes -- or if it is a multi-model model, then we apply thee decay 
functions based on the modes specified. The do that, pass the current time, the time of each row in the ground, and the 
mode of each row in the ground to a function that computes the decays. We use matrix multiplication to apply the vector 
of decays to the ground codes.

Once the decays are added, we process the data much like ENA: there is a window (the ground) and a response, we do 
matrix multiplication and then subtract the response-to-response diagonal so we are not counting self-references within 
the response line.

A weighting function is then applied (default is sqrt), to account for the same weighting issues that come up in a 
weighted ENA model of over-weighting rows with high code-counts.

TMA does this as a directed matrix, and then at the very end, the undirected matrix is computed from the directed. Both 
are returned.

Finally, the function converts the adjacency matrices (directed and undirected) into a table of adjacency vectors.

Information needed to make an ENA set with the undirected adjacency vectors is passed to ena.set to construct a 
properly-formatted ENA set. ~~*Note: this does not work at the moment, but Cody is going to look into it.*~~

All of the above functionality should work. That is, models can be run as uni- or multi-modal, with or without time limits on the lookback, with or without meta data.

# Test Accumulation #1

To test the model, I created two delay functions. One is the original decay function. One has a longer decay time.


```{r TMAaccumulation}

#this tests the main accumulation function for TMA

#original decay function
chat.decay.function = decay.function

#decay function with a longer decay time
view.decay.function = function(x) return(-0.0039*x^3 + 0.0661*x^2 - 0.3507*x + 1)


#construct list for passing to accumulate,units
modal.decay.function = list()
modal.decay.function$view = view.decay.function
modal.decay.function$chat = chat.decay.function

my.accumulation = accumulate.units(context.object = these.hoos, 
                                   codes = c('Data',
                                              'Technical.Constraints',
                                              'Performance.Parameters',
                                              'Client.and.Consultant.Requests',
                                              'Design.Reasoning',
                                              'Collaboration'
                                              ), 
                                   time.column = "time", 
                                   #decay.function = decay.function, 
                                   decay.function = modal.decay.function, 
                                   mode.column = "CommunicationType",
                                   weight.by = sqrt,
                                   time.limit = 7,
                                   meta.data = c("CONFIDENCE.Pre", "CONFIDENCE.Change"),
                                   return.ena.set = TRUE)
```

# Define Decay Functions

Some example chat and view decay functions.

```{r testMaskAndTraditionalWindowModel}
#window decay function, window size = 4
chat.decay.function = function(x) {ifelse(x<4, 1, 0)}

#decay function with a bigger window size
view.decay.function = function(x) {ifelse(x<20, 1, 0)}
```

_Note: Seems like this could be a single function a la:_

```
decay.function <- function(x, n = 4) {
  ifelse(x < n, 1, 0)
}

# If needed, the same `chat.decay` and `view.decay` can be used, while still using the parameterized function:

chat.decay.function <- function(x) decay.function(x, 4)
view.decay.function <- function(x) decay.function(x, 20)
```
